entries.title: generate releases from commits, on a release train
entries.body:
The account of what changed moves from a file maintained by hand to the
commits themselves, because the commits are what a release contains and a
hand-maintained file drifts from them.

scripts/changelog-gen.mjs walks the log since the last tag and writes
changelog/<version>.json: one file per release, carrying every entry's type,
scope, breaking flag, title, prose body, measurements, refs, tests, commits,
author and date, plus the release's range and artifacts. That JSON is the
record and the website reads it; CHANGELOG.md and the GitHub release notes are
rendered from it, so there is one account of a release and two views of it,
which cannot drift.

The subject gives the heading and the version bump, the body gives the prose.
Subject-only generators throw the body away, which is the half worth keeping
here -- the explanation of why a lowering is the way it is. `Measured:`,
`Refs:` and `Tests:` trailers become structured fields, and `Release-Note:`
replaces a body written for the reviewer rather than the reader. Co-authorship
and session trailers are stripped from every body: they are bookkeeping, not
what changed. A subject that is not conventional is filed under
"Uncategorised" with its body intact and reported, because a release that
silently omits a change is worse than one with an untidy heading.

The train: every merge to main refreshes one open "Release <version>" pull
request carrying the bump, the JSON and the rendered section; merging it
creates the tag; the tag builds and publishes. The notes are reviewed in the
pull request whose body is those notes, before anyone can read them. The bump
touches self/branding.ts as well as package.json, because tests/run.js fails
when the two disagree and the release PR would otherwise be red at itself.

release.yml now publishes from the reviewed JSON rather than a fresh walk of
the log, caps a body over 120,000 characters at a paragraph boundary, and
fails on an empty one. That last check is not hypothetical: with CHANGELOG.md
emptied, `changelog-section.sh 0.1.0` fell back to an empty [Unreleased] and
exited 0, so the release would have shipped a blank body.

pr-title.yml checks the pull request title, since squash-merge makes it the
commit subject. It shells out to the generator's own --check-subject so CI
enforces exactly what the generator parses, rather than a second copy of the
rule that can drift from it; the title is passed through the environment
rather than interpolated into the shell.

changelog/0.1.0.json is generated from the 181 commits behind this branch.
All 181 predate the convention and are filed as "Uncategorised" with their
bodies intact, which is the migration working as intended rather than a gap.

npm run check and npm test green: 1212 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped.
entries.author: Claude

entries.title: regenerate the stage1 goldens for the corpus WP25 left
entries.body:
Merging main brought WP25, which removes inheritance from the language and
with it five programs from the corpus -- the four `cls_extends_*` cases and
the cookbook's `cls_inheritance.ts` -- and adds `cls_implements_prefix.ts` for
the widened `implements`. The goldens added on this branch were generated
before that merge, so they recorded a corpus that no longer exists and the
check failed on 262 programs against 259.

That is the check working. Regenerated only after confirming the four oracles
it succeeds still agree on the merged tree -- checker 316/316 files, IR
325/325 programs, types 119/119, diagnostics 570/570, symbols 25/25 -- because
a golden regenerated while the two compilers disagree records a bug as the
specification. The diff is the five programs leaving, the one arriving, and
self/ itself losing the inheritance it no longer compiles.

Four status claims in MASTER_PLAN went stale in the same merge and are
corrected here: M4's contents (WP2b has left the milestone rather than been
finished), wave 3's state, the "one piece still outstanding" sentence, and the
open decision on class inheritance, which WP25 closes as "none". The paragraph
main added to §9 covers the language change; these four are the status rows it
did not reach.

changelog/0.1.0.json is regenerated over the merged history: 186 entries, the
four commits from main carrying their bodies intact.
entries.author: Claude

entries.title: start at 0.0.0 and stop pinning the version in goldens
entries.body:
package.json, package-lock.json and self/branding.ts go to 0.0.0, which is
what lets the release train cut the first release itself rather than needing
0.1.0 tagged by hand: it computes the next version rather than the current
one, so a tree already claiming 0.1.0 left it nothing to compute.

The first release is 0.1.0 whatever the commits say. Every commit predating
the convention is typed `other`, so a type-driven bump reads the whole history
as a patch and ships 0.0.1 -- a number claiming the compiler is a bug fix on
nothing. `changelog-gen.mjs` special-cases "no previous tag" to 0.1.0, which is
also the base case the seed policy already names (docs/wp12-release.md).

Two surfaces pinned the version inside checked-in goldens, and both are
structural defects rather than stale files: `-g` writes the version into the
DWARF producer, so `dbg_locals` and `dbg_result` carried "nish 0.1.0"; and the
checker folds module constants, so the stage1 dump carried self/branding.ts's
VERSION. Either one means the release pull request -- the commit whose whole
job is to bump the version -- is red at itself, and a release cannot go green
on its own bump.

Both are now normalised to "<version>" the way tests/run.js already normalises
the working directory to <root>, and for the same reason one step further out:
the version is the compiler's identity, not a fact about a lowering. It stays
pinned where it belongs, by the --version checks and by the
branding/package.json equality check. Verified by simulating a bump to 0.2.0:
every golden stayed green, then reverted.

CHANGELOG.md goes back to a header and an empty [Unreleased], and
changelog/0.1.0.json is removed: both are the train's to write, and a [0.1.0]
section before the tag contradicts the header that says this file is
generated. The [Unreleased] link points at the history rather than at a v0.1.0
that does not exist. README no longer claims a version the tree does not have.

Every CI gate green at 0.0.0: check, test (1179 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped),
smoke, the IR cookbook staleness check, the diagnostic-code registry check,
and the documentation link check.
entries.author: Claude

entries.title: give the release pull request a conventional title
entries.body:
* ci(release): give the release pull request a conventional title

The release train opened its pull request as `Release 0.1.0`, which the
repository's own `pr-title.yml` rejects: the title is the squash-merge
subject, and `scripts/changelog-gen.mjs --check-subject` does not classify
it. The release pull request would therefore have landed with a red check
on the one pull request nobody can rewrite by hand, and -- had it been
merged anyway -- the release commit would have gone into the *next* set of
notes under "Uncategorised".

It is now `chore(release): <version>`, which is what the merge subject
should have said all along: it passes the title check like any other pull
request, and the generator files it under "Chores".

Refs: docs/wp12-release.md#release-procedure

* ci(release): stop a blocked `gh pr create` from painting main red

Every push to main failed the release train:

    pull request create failed: GraphQL: GitHub Actions is not permitted
    to create or approve pull requests (createPullRequest)

That refusal is a repository switch -- Settings > Actions > General >
Workflow permissions > "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull
requests" -- and no `permissions:` block in a workflow can grant it. The
job had already done everything else: the version bump, the JSON and the
rendered section were committed and `release/next` was pushed. The only
missing artifact was the pull request itself, and the failure repeated
identically on every merge, saying nothing new each time.

So the step now tells the three outcomes apart. A successful create is a
notice as before. That one refusal becomes a warning carrying the switch
to turn on and the compare link that opens the pull request in one click,
and the job succeeds -- the release costs a click rather than being
blocked, and main stays green. Any *other* `gh pr create` failure still
exits 1, because it is not a known and benign one.

A `RELEASE_PR_TOKEN` secret (a PAT or app token with `repo`) lifts the
restriction outright; the step prefers it over the default token when the
repository has one, and needs no other change to run unattended.

Tests: the step's four paths (create, refusal, other failure, refresh an
open pull request) driven against a stubbed `gh` -- exit 0, 0, 1, 0.
Refs: docs/wp12-release.md#release-procedure
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: regenerate the benchmark report against Go and Rust
entries.body:
`node bench/run.mjs --runs 15 --warmup 3` over all seven programs with
every toolchain present (clang 18.1.3, rustc 1.94.1, go 1.24.7). The
checksums agree first: 47 binaries across the four languages at the
validation sizes, and all seven at full size, so the columns compare the
same computation rather than four programs that merely look alike.

Nish is ahead of Go on all seven programs, and inside the 1.10x WP9
target against Rust `-O3` on five of the seven. `result` remains the
outlier wp17-result-abi.md §4 predicts, and `nbody` sits just outside.

The host is not the one the previous report was measured on — a 2.8 GHz
Xeon rather than a 2.1 GHz one — so the absolute milliseconds do not
compare with the run this replaces. wp9-optimisation.md's warning about
a single run on a shared virtual machine applies to every ratio within
15-20 % of parity; only sieve, strbuild and `result` are far enough from
the line to be read on one run.

This also corrects a stale size table. The three `--number-mode f64`
binaries roughly double here (nbody 10,856 -> 21,184, spectral 9,504 ->
19,816, vec3 8,040 -> 18,368) while the four programs that never format
a double are unchanged. That is not a regression taken in this run: it
is the Ryu trade bb346d1 made deliberately and recorded in
wp15-performance.md §7a, whose two power-of-five tables are 9,888 bytes
of `.rodata` that section GC links only into a binary that formats a
double. Rebuilding bench/nbody at bb346d1~1 gives 10,856 bytes exactly,
and at HEAD 21,184, so the numbers this report replaces were measured on
a tree without Ryu even though the commit recording them came after it.
bb346d1 predicted 21,168 for nbody; the remaining 16 bytes are later
commits.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: build the notes from conventional commits only
entries.body:
The first release rendered 5,378 lines of `CHANGELOG.md` from 175 commits,
and 171 of them -- 97% of the file -- were never meant to be read as release
notes: the work-in-progress history behind a merge commit, and the commits
that predate the convention. They landed under "Uncategorised" with their
full bodies, on the reasoning that a release which silently omits a change
is worse than one with an untidy heading.

That reasoning holds for the omission and not for the bucket. The notes are
the account of what a release changed, and a commit that never said what it
changed is not that account -- the subject that did land already has an
entry of its own, so the branch behind it is the same change told twice.

`scripts/changelog-gen.mjs` now skips a subject it cannot classify instead
of filing it. Nothing goes missing quietly: every skipped subject is listed
on stderr with its sha, and `--include-unconventional` restores the previous
behaviour byte for byte for a release that wants the raw history. Prose that
belongs above the sections goes in `changelog/<version>.intro.md`, which is
the better place for it. A range whose commits are all unconventional now
fails saying so, rather than with the old "no commits in range".

Two smaller things fall out. GitHub's squash-merge rule -- the `---------`
it writes above the co-authorship trailers when a branch had more than one
commit -- sits before the trailers rather than at the end, so `splitTrailers`
left it in the prose and it rendered as a stray horizontal rule in the middle
of an entry; it is stripped now. And `--next`, which answers a version and
nothing else, no longer repeats the skip listing that the `--write` call a
line later in the same job already prints.

Measured: 5,378 -> 168 lines rendered over the same range; 175 -> 4 entries
Refs: docs/wp12-release.md#release-procedure
Tests: tests/run.js "WP12: changelog" -- eight checks against a throwaway
repository holding a conventional commit, a work-in-progress commit and a
branch merged rather than squashed, covering the filter, the stderr listing,
--include-unconventional, the all-unconventional failure and --check-subject
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: add arithmetic and arena-drop performance warnings
entries.body:
* feat(checker): warn on dropped allocations and on provable overflow

Four new WP15 §8 warnings, on by default, never fatal, silenced together by
`--no-warn-performance`, and mirrored word for word in both compilers.

**An allocation dropped by an assignment** (NL9003). `p = new Point(n)` where
`p` was declared holding an allocation of its own: the value it held is
unreachable from there and nothing frees it. Worse, assigning a local is what
takes away the proof WP6's automatic arena scope needs, so the function loses
its `nish_arena_mark` / `nish_arena_release` bracket entirely and *every*
allocation in the body — including the ones that were going to be stack slots
— lives until the program exits. This is the warning that answers "the
compiler could not prove it, so the memory is simply never freed" with a line
number, and it names both rewrites: a `const` per value, or an explicit
`Arena.mark()` / `Arena.release(m)` bracket where the assignment is the point.

**Arithmetic that provably goes wrong** (NL9004-NL9006): a constant `+`, `-`
or `*` over decimal literals whose value does not fit the `i32` it is computed
in, reported on the innermost expression that overflows and silent under
`--wrapping`, where the wrap is the defined answer; `toI64(a * b)` on `i32`
operands, where the multiplication has already wrapped by the time the
conversion widens it; and a shift by a literal count at or beyond the operand
width, which is masked and so never the shift that was written.

Signed overflow is undefined behaviour by default, so warning wherever it is
*possible* would mean warning on every `+` and every `*` in the program. §8 is
explicit that a warning nobody can act on trains people to ignore the class,
so each rule fires only where the compiler can point at the value or at a
shape whose rewrite is mechanical, and the unsigned widths stay silent because
they are defined to wrap.

Two guards came from running the rules over this compiler's own source rather
than from reasoning. The widening rule started on `+`, `-` and `*` and
immediately flagged `toI64(intBits(type) - 1)`, which has nothing wrong with
it; it is multiplication-only now. The dropped-allocation rule started on any
assignment and flagged `let what = "unbound"` followed by three branches that
each assign a template — real retention, but assigning a local in a branch is
how a language without a match expression computes a value, and there is
nothing to rewrite. Requiring the declaration to allocate as well leaves
exactly the case where an allocation is dropped.

The fold is bounded so that it can never itself overflow the `i64` stage1
folds in — a fold that overflowed inside the check that reports overflow would
be undefined behaviour in the diagnostic — and the bound is 2^52, which is
also the largest power of two either compiler can write, since a literal past
2^53 cannot be spelled exactly.

`scripts/gen-diagnostic-codes.mjs` now skips `src/checker/performance.ts` and
takes the whole class from its hand-written list: every message in that file
is a band 9 warning, and extracting them would have put a second, unreachable
entry for each in the error table — and moved NL9001 and NL9002, which are
promised stable.

Measured: 2 dropped allocations and 0 false positives over the 54 modules of self/
Refs: docs/wp15-performance.md, docs/LANGUAGE.md#diagnostics-and-debugging-flags
Tests: tests/cases/perf_arena_drop, perf_arena_quiet, perf_overflow, perf_overflow_const, perf_overflow_wrapping, perf_overflow_quiet

* docs(readme): state the memory-safety guarantee and what it resembles

The memory strategy was documented as an implementation detail under
"Performance and binary size", which answers how it works and not what it
guarantees. The question readers actually arrive with is what the guarantee
*is*, and which language it is like.

A new "Memory safety" section answers both. The guarantee, as a table of bug
classes: use-after-free and double free are not expressible, because nothing
is freed individually and the four placement mechanisms decide lifetimes at
compile time; every `a[i]`, `a[i] op= v`, `charCodeAt` and `pop` is
bounds-checked with an unsigned compare, so a negative index fails too; `T |
null` is a separate type whose narrowing the checker enforces, which is what
licenses `nonnull dereferenceable` everywhere else; `new Array<T>(n)`
zero-fills and refuses pointer element types; and nothing unwinds.

The comparison is answered plainly rather than claimed for one family:
memory-safe like Go, allocated like Zig, errors like Rust, nulls like Kotlin,
overflow like C. The two C-shaped holes -- signed overflow undefined by
default, and `Arena.reset` / `Arena.release` unchecked -- are named in the
same breath as the guarantee rather than left to a footnote, along with
`--unchecked-indexing` and the interop boundary.

The part worth writing down is what happens when the analysis *fails*, which
is where designs actually differ: Rust refuses to compile it, Go falls back
to the garbage collector, Zig hands the question back to you and an
allocator, and this compiler leaves the value in the arena until `main`
returns. That is what makes `src/codegen/escape.ts` an optimisation and never
a correctness device, and it is the trade the whole memory design rests on.

Refs: docs/wp6-memory.md, docs/LANGUAGE.md#memory-model

* docs(checker): write down the arena-scope gap the warning leaves open

The dropped-allocation warning (NL9003) reports a local assigned an
allocation over one it already held. A local declared holding a literal and
then given its one value in a branch — `let what = "unbound"` and three arms
that each assign a template — is the same retention with none of the
actionability: `allocLeaks` goes on, the arena scope is not emitted, and
everything the body allocated lives until `main` returns, but there is no
rewrite to name, because assigning a local in a branch is how a language
without a match expression computes a value.

Silence there was a deliberate reading of the §8 bar, and an undocumented
deliberate silence is indistinguishable from a bug. It is now written down in
three places: `wp6-memory.md` under "Left out" as the memory limitation it
is, with the two ways to close it — a "captured only into one binding" fact
in the escape analysis, which would need a stack rule that does not require a
fixed binding, or an opt-in `--report-arena` audit that prints every
allocation site with its placement rather than warning about it; in
`LANGUAGE.md`, where the rule's guards are listed and a reader could
otherwise take the guard for a guarantee; and in `wp15-performance.md` §8,
where it is the worked example of the bar cutting both ways.

Refs: docs/wp6-memory.md, docs/wp15-performance.md

* fix(checker): make both compilers agree on the new warnings

Three defects found reviewing the branch, all of them divergences between
stage0 and stage1 or claims the code does not check, and none of them caught
by the oracles: 322/322 files agree because no program in the corpus uses a
hexadecimal shift count or reassigns a hole-less template.

**Literal spellings.** `ts.NumericLiteral.text` is normalised -- `0x20`
arrives as `"32"`, `100_000` as `"100000"`, `1e2` as `"100"` -- so testing it
for decimal digits folded exactly the spellings stage1 refuses, and `a <<
0x20` warned on one side and not the other. Stage0 reads the literal as
written now, which is what stage1 has always done, and
`docs/LANGUAGE.md` stops contradicting the code.

**Hole-less templates.** The stage1 parser gives `N_TEMPLATE` to `` `hello` ``
as well as `` `a${b}` ``, where stage0's `ts.isTemplateExpression` excludes
the first. `let s = \`hello\`; s = \`world\`;` therefore warned under stage1
alone, about two string literals that allocate nothing. The stage1 test now
asks for a part that is not template text, which is the test `accumulates`
next door already uses.

**An unchecked claim.** The dropped-allocation message says "nothing can
reach the old value from here" and nothing verified it: `out.push(row); row =
"c" + "d";` in a loop warned although every value it drops is live in `out`,
and the `const` rewrite it names does not compile there.

The guard this wants is not "is the local ever captured" -- that would be
wrong in the other direction, and this compiler's own `astLines` is the proof.
It builds a line, replaces it in a branch, and only then pushes it: the
replaced value really is dead and both warnings there are right. What
separates the two is order, so the guard is about order. Inside a loop, a
capture anywhere in the outermost enclosing loop counts, because control comes
back around to the assignment with the capture behind it. Outside one, only a
capture that finishes before the assignment starts can have taken the value
the assignment is about to drop.

`perf_overflow_spelling` pins the first two on both sides -- and ships without
a `.out`, like `perf_overflow_const`, because `100_000 * 100_000` is an
overflowing signed `*` under the default `nsw` and a golden that runs
undefined behaviour pins whatever LLVM did that week. `perf_arena_quiet` grows
the push-then-reassign loop and the hole-less template.

Tests: tests/cases/perf_overflow_spelling, perf_arena_quiet

* test(self): drop the separator spelling from perf_overflow_spelling

`100_000` in that case turned the stage1 oracle red, and for a reason that has
nothing to do with folding: stage0 accepts a numeric separator, as
`docs/LANGUAGE.md` says it should, and stage1 refuses it with `Non-integer
literal \`100_000\` in i32 number mode`. Three lines reproduce it with no
warning in sight:

```ts
export function main(): number {
  const n = 1_000;
  return n;
}
```

So the separator is out of the case and a comment says why it is missing,
which is the part worth keeping: a reader who notices the gap should find the
reason rather than assume an oversight. `0x20` and `1e5` still carry the rule
-- both would warn if either compiler folded the spelling, and neither does.

The divergence itself is left alone here. It is in the number path rather than
in a diagnostic, it needs its own tests, and it can break a bootstrap, none of
which belongs in a pull request about warnings.

Tests: tests/cases/perf_overflow_spelling

* test(self): reduce perf_overflow_spelling to spellings stage1 gets right

`1e5` turned the IR oracle red, and not because either compiler folded it:
stage0 emits `mul nsw i32 100000, 100000` and stage1 emits `mul nsw i32 245,
245`. `parseIntegerLiteral` in `self/constants.ts` accepts a hex letter as a
digit whatever the radix is, so base ten reads `e` as 14 — `1*10 + 14` is 24,
then `24*10 + 5` is 245 — and a character that is not a digit at all is
skipped rather than refused, so nothing about the literal is ever reported.

`docs/LANGUAGE.md` accepts decimal, hexadecimal, binary, octal, exponent and
separated literals. Measured against that, stage1 handles two of the six:

| literal | stage0 | stage1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `1e5` | 100000 | **245** |
| `1e3` | 1000 | **243** |
| `0b101` | 5 | `Literal does not fit in i32` |
| `0o17` | 15 | `Literal does not fit in i32` |
| `1_000` | 1000 | `Non-integer literal` |
| `0x20` | 32 | 32 |

`parseIntegerLiteral` itself handles `_`, `0b` and `0o` correctly, so the three
rejections come from a decimal-only check that runs ahead of it; the two paths
disagree about what a literal is, which is what produces a wrong rejection in
one place and a wrong value in another.

None of that is this rule's doing, and a case that fails for an unrelated
reason is a case nobody can read, so the case keeps `0x20` — which still
carries the rule it was written for, since folding the normalised text would
report a masked shift there — and a comment records the other five and why
they are absent. The divergence wants its own change: the number path, with
conformance tests for every spelling on both sides, and a bootstrap to re-check
afterwards.

Tests: tests/cases/perf_overflow_spelling
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: unstick the `---` rule and render the notes as an index
entries.body:
Two things about the release pull request's body.

The rule between the preamble and the notes rendered as `---### Fixed`,
one line of literal text. The notes arrived through a `$(...)`, and
command substitution eats trailing newlines, so appending them to a
preamble that ended in the rule left nothing between the two. They are
now an argument to the single `printf` that writes the blank lines.

And a section is an index rather than an account: one line per change --
the scope, the subject, and a link to the pull request it landed in, or
to the commit when it landed without one -- under the heading its type
gives. The commit bodies, the `Measured:` numbers and the refs stay in
`changelog/<version>.json`, which is what the website renders an entry
from; inlined, they turned one release into pages of prose that nobody
scrolled, when the pull request is already where the rest is. The link
target is read from `package.json#repository`, so a fork renders its
own links rather than this repository's.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: give a concise arrow body the context a `return` has
entries.body:
* fix(checker): give a concise arrow body the context a `return` has

WP22 §4 said a concise arrow body (`=> expr`) "is checked and emitted
exactly as the block form with one `return`". That held for the checker's
own `checkReturnValue` and failed everywhere else, because two kinds of
pass decide what a `return` is by climbing to the parent node — and a
concise body's parent is the arrow, not a `ReturnStatement`.

**Contextual typing.** Three walks stopped at `ts.isReturnStatement`:
`contextualType` in `checker/classes.ts` (an object literal's struct, and
a class value converting to an interface it implements), `contextualType`
in `checker/arrays.ts` (the element type of `[]`), and `contextType` in
`checker/math.ts` (a numeric literal's width). So all four of these were
rejected while every block-bodied twin compiled:

    const swap = (p: Pair): Pair => ({ first: p.second, second: p.first });
    const asPair = (o: Ordered): Pair => o;
    const full = (): u8 => 255;
    const empty = (): i32[] => [];

**The call-site reclaim**, which is the one that did not announce itself.
`flowTarget` in `codegen/escape.ts` read a returned allocation as a local,
so `allocates` came out false for the callee and WP9's `nish_arena_mark` /
`nish_arena_keep` bracket disappeared from every call to it — not an error,
just a function whose temporaries now live for the life of the program.

Both are one predicate, `isFunctionResult`: the operand of a `return`, or
the body an arrow *is*.

Stage1 had exactly one of the two, and which one is the useful part. Its
checker threads the wanted type down as `want` rather than climbing, so the
first was never reachable there; its `flowTarget` does climb, so it had the
second, and `self/escape.ts` takes the same fix. Until now the two compilers
silently disagreed about programs no test had written.

Found by rewriting `docs/cookbook/` to the arrow form and diffing the
emitted IR: `mem_reclaim` was the listing that lost its bracket.

Refs: docs/wp22-arrow-functions.md#8a, docs/LANGUAGE.md#functions
Tests: tests/cases/fn_arrow_concise

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01RKwbr1PL1fMW2qFnQa1H4P

* docs: declare every shown function as an arrow

WP22 §10 left one thing to confirm before the migration could start:
whether `export const main = (): number => ...` becomes the first line of
every example, every README and every cookbook entry. It does. This is
stage C's documentation half — everything a reader is shown, and nothing
the bootstrap gates.

Rewritten: `README.md`, `docs/LANGUAGE.md`, `docs/INSTALL.md`,
`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, all 68 `docs/cookbook/*.ts` (so every listing in
`docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md`), `examples/` and `examples/multi/`, the playground
in `web/`, `docs/wp18-generics.md` — whose rewrite §9 asked for so that
note and this one would not contradict each other — and the `.claude/`
rules, which still told an agent the language has no arrow functions.

**The goldens are the proof, not the cost.** Every cookbook snippet and
every example was compiled before and after: the emitted `.ll` is
byte-identical in all of them, which is what §2 predicted and what makes a
rewrite this size checkable at all. The two places the IR did move are
compiler bugs the rewrite exposed, fixed in the commit before this one.

Two mechanical consequences. `scripts/smoke.sh` selected programs with
`grep -E '^export function main'`, so the arrow entry points made it find
none; it now accepts either spelling, as `tests/run.js` already did. And
`useConsistentArrowReturn` is an error in `biome.json`, so a single-`return`
body is now written concise — which is how the contextual-typing bug came
to be found at all.

`--help` and the `--link` refusal name `export const main` too, on both
compilers. The two diagnostics that still say `export function main` stay:
`scripts/gen-diagnostic-codes.mjs` keys a stable code on message text, so
rewording them retires NL2229 and NL2149 for a spelling change. They belong
with stage D, which makes the other spelling wrong.

Still `function`, and deliberately: `self/` (603 declarations, which §8
wants in a commit of its own so the bootstrap is the only thing under
test), `tests/cases/` and the other corpora, `bench/`, and the historical
wp1-wp17 notes.

Refs: docs/wp22-arrow-functions.md
Tests: docs/cookbook/regen.sh --check, scripts/smoke.sh

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01RKwbr1PL1fMW2qFnQa1H4P

entries.title: close the last two gaps in the benchmark suite
entries.body:
* perf(codegen): give a private `Result` one slot per arm, not one shared payload

`bench/result` sat at 1.84x behind Rust `-O3` and level with its own C twin,
and the whole gap was one instruction.

WP15 §7b already split the discriminant out of the packed word for a
non-exported function — `{ i1, i32 }`, rustc's `ScalarPair` — but left both
payloads sharing the one `i32`. Sharing the slot means the ok arm and the
error arm are still never separate SSA values, which is exactly what
[wp17-result-abi.md](docs/wp17-result-abi.md) §4's four-way table blamed:
`half`'s `Err(n)` and `Ok(n / 2)` meet in a single value, so once `half` is
inlined the value the ok path reads is `phi(n, n >> 1)`, and instcombine folds
that to a *variable* shift `n >> (1 - odd)`. The enclosing `select` cannot
recover the constant shift — nothing propagates "on this arm `odd` is 0" into
a shift amount — so the loop carries three instructions it computes only to
discard. Patching that one `lshr` in the optimised `.ll` and changing nothing
else took the benchmark from 472 ms to 256 ms, which is what said the shape
was the cause rather than the code generation.

The private ABI is now `{ i1, i32, i32 }`: the tag and one slot per arm, with
the arm that is not live left `undef`. That removes the `phi` instead of
fighting the fold — `phi(undef, n >> 1)` is `n >> 1` — and the shift is
constant again. The IR also gets shorter: a `return Ok(v)` is one
`insertvalue` where it was `zext`/`shl`/`or` and then a split back out of the
word.

Only functions with `internal` linkage are affected. The packed `i64` every
host sees is untouched, `packArm` / `packObject` / `unpackResult` still serve
it, and `privateResultAbi` is still exactly `strictExports && !exported`, so
`--emit-header`, `--emit-dts` and `--emit-napi` describe the ABI they always
did and `res_export` still emits `i64` for all four of its shapes.

One attribute had to go with it. The dead arm's slot is `undef` by
construction and `noundef` on an aggregate is about every element of it, so
`paramAttributes` and `returnAttributes` no longer emit `noundef` for a
by-value `Result` under the private ABI — the one shape in the language that
is not fully defined. Measured at no cost.

Measured: 464 ms to 218 ms on bench/result; 1.84x behind Rust -O3 to 1.00x
Refs: docs/wp17-result-abi.md, docs/wp15-performance.md, docs/wp9-optimisation.md
Tests: tests/cases/res_by_value, res_by_value_param, res_by_value_payloads, res_by_value_propagate, dbg_result

* docs(bench): regenerate the benchmark report

`node bench/run.mjs --runs 15 --warmup 3` after the private `Result` ABI
gained a slot per arm. `result` is the row that moved: 1.84x behind Rust
`-O3` to **1.00x**, with the same minimum and the same median as the Rust
column (218 / 263 ms) and its own C twin at 405 / 485.

Six of the seven programs are now inside the 1.10x target against Rust —
sieve 0.89x, strbuild 0.92x, vec3 0.93x, spectral 1.00x, result 1.00x, fib
1.03x — and nbody at 1.23x is the only one outside it. Nish is ahead of Go on
all seven. The rest of the table moved with the host rather than with the
compiler: this run is on a 2.1 GHz Xeon where the last was on a 2.8 GHz one,
and the medians sit well above the minima either way, so read the ratios with
§"Where these numbers stand today" of docs/wp9-optimisation.md in mind.

Refs: docs/wp9-optimisation.md, docs/wp17-result-abi.md

* perf(codegen): give class field access TBAA metadata

`bench/nbody` was the last row outside the WP9 target, at 1.23x behind Rust
`-O3`, and the cause was not code generation. It was that LLVM cannot tell
two `%struct.Body*` values apart: a store to `bi.vx` and a load of `bj.mass`
are both "a double behind a pointer", so every store to `bi` killed every
later load from `bj`. The inner loop of `advance` reloaded `bj.mass` once per
component, could not hoist `bi.mass` or `bi.x`/`.y`/`.z` out of the loop at
all, and did not vectorise.

One control experiment says it is alias information rather than our lowering.
Instructions retired, counted with callgrind so there is no spread to argue
about:

    C -O3                        80,344,647
    Rust -O3                     82,132,809
    Nish, before                 87,514,731
    C -O3 -fno-strict-aliasing   93,394,660

The last row is the same compiler on the same source with only its alias
information taken away, and it does *more* work than we did.

So class field loads and stores now carry `!tbaa`, in clang's struct-path
shape: a root, an `omnipotent char`, a scalar node per LLVM type, a struct
node listing the layout, and an access tag naming the class, the type and the
byte offset. A `double` at offset 48 of a `Body` is then not the `double` at
offset 24 of a `Body`, whoever points at it. `bj.mass` is loaded once, the
`bi` fields leave the loop, and the checksum is unchanged bit for bit.

**Why it is sound is the absence of two things.** Nish has no inheritance
(WP25) and no casts, unions or pointer arithmetic, so a `%struct.C*` is the
only type through which a `C` object's bytes are ever read or written, and two
distinct classes never overlap. The exception is `implements`, which lays an
interface's fields out first so that `%struct.C*` may be `bitcast` to
`%struct.I*` — real prefix subtyping, and the case C++ handles by making the
base its first member. Rather than model it, `fieldTbaa` emits no tag for an
interface or for any class that implements one; an access without `!tbaa` may
alias everything, which is the conservative answer. It costs nothing measured:
the shapes this exists for are plain classes.

Measured: bench/nbody 87,514,731 instructions to 80,014,745 — the lowest of the
four — and 1.23x behind Rust -O3 to 0.96x. vec3 and spectral retire exactly the
same count as before, to the instruction: they have no two-pointers-into-one-
type question to answer.
Refs: docs/wp9-optimisation.md, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md
Tests: tests/cases/cls_point, cls_vector, cls_field_write, cls_nested, mem_stack_struct, dbg_locals

* docs(bench): regenerate the benchmark report

`node bench/run.mjs --runs 15 --warmup 3` after class field access gained
`!tbaa`. nbody is the row that moved: **1.23x behind Rust `-O3` to 0.96x**,
and it is now faster than its C twin as well (737 ms against 767).

**Every one of the seven is at or inside the 1.10x target against Rust for the
first time** — sieve 0.81x, strbuild 0.86x, vec3 0.95x, nbody 0.96x, spectral
1.00x, result 1.00x — with fib's 1.15x the one number to read against the
run-to-run spread rather than as a result: re-measured on the same binaries,
interleaved, it is 261 ms against Rust's 262, and it retires fewer
instructions than either C or Rust. Nish is ahead of Go on all seven.

Refs: docs/wp9-optimisation.md
